subtitle: Repeated trouble follows repeated choices

stick.excerpt: This time, however, he presented Anansi with a fine stick and bade him good-bye. Anansi could scarcely wait till he got into the boat—so anxious was he to try the magic properties of his new gift. “Stick, stick,” he said, “what you used to do for your master do for me also.” The stick began to beat him so severely that, in a few minutes, he was obliged to jump into the water and swim ashore, leaving boat and stick to drift away where they pleased. Then he returned sorrowfully homeward, bemoaning his many bruises and wishing he had acted more wisely from the beginning.
stick.note: Verbatim text from Barker and Sinclair's 1917 English collection of Gold Coast stories. Attribute any specific community only where the collection does so.

narrativeBlocks.title: A second gift
narrativeBlocks.body: In this Gold Coast story, Anansi returns to Thunder's cottage. Thunder gives him a stick and warns him of its magic.

narrativeBlocks.title: An instruction ignored
narrativeBlocks.body: Quotation from Barker and Sinclair's English collection (whitespace normalized): “This time, however, he presented Anansi with a fine stick and bade him good-bye. Anansi could scarcely wait till he got into the boat—so anxious was he to try the magic properties of his new gift. “Stick, stick,” he said, “what you used to do for your master do for me also.” The stick began to beat him so severely that, in a few minutes, he was obliged to jump into the water and swim ashore, leaving boat and stick to drift away where they pleased. Then he returned sorrowfully homeward, bemoaning his many bruises and wishing he had acted more wisely from the beginning.”

narrativeBlocks.title: The stick turns on Anansi
narrativeBlocks.body: Anansi tries to command the stick to do for him what it did for Thunder. It beats him until he jumps into the water and swims ashore.

narrativeBlocks.title: A folktale's moral is not ethnography
narrativeBlocks.body: Barker and Sinclair retell this as one story in a Gold Coast collection. Its magical stick and comic punishment are narrative details, not evidence of a universal religious practice.

narrativeBlocks.title: Repeated choices matter
narrativeBlocks.body: The episode frames Anansi's misfortune as a consequence of how he uses the gifts, not as a general account of Thunder worship.
